Building a lineage service is mostly about deciding what not to compute. The first time I watched our DAG explode under a backfill, the instinct was to add more workers. That instinct is usually wrong. Throughput problems in lineage systems are almost never about raw CPU. They are about fan-out, about how a single ALTER TABLE cascades into thousands of column-level edges, and about whether you materialize those edges before anyone asks.

We keep Iceberg snapshots as the source of truth for table shape. Spark jobs write metadata; a lightweight watcher tails the snapshot log and emits a compact event: table id, snapshot id, schema hash. The consumer is deliberately boring. It does not walk the whole graph. It asks one question: did the schema hash change? If not, we skip. If yes, we recompute only the columns whose types or names moved. This is the unglamorous half of incremental computation, and it is the half that keeps the pager quiet.

People love to talk about knowledge graphs as if they were cathedrals. In production they are warehouses with forklifts. You need idempotent upserts, a dead-letter queue, and a way to rebuild a partition without locking readers. We blue-green the Nebula space for that reason. The importer writes into the cold space, we flip a pointer, and the hot space becomes eligible for compaction. Rollback is a pointer flip in the other direction. It is not elegant. It is operationally boring, which is the highest compliment I can give a data path.

Column lineage is where the abstraction starts to leak. A SQL expression is not a column. It is a tree. `COALESCE(a, b)` is not "a" and it is not "b". If you flatten too early you lose the join key that an analyst will later swear was obvious. We keep the expression tree in a sidecar table and only promote edges that survive a stability window: seen in three consecutive runs, or explicitly marked by a human. False positives in lineage are worse than false negatives. A missing edge is a gap. A phantom edge is a lie that will be quoted in an incident review.

The watcher used to parse every query with a full SQL parser. That was a mistake. Most queries are trivial projections. We now run a cheap regex prefilter: if the statement has no JOIN, no UNION, and no subquery, we take the column list from the INSERT and move on. The expensive parser still exists. It is a fallback, not a default. Latency dropped from seconds to tens of milliseconds for the common case. The remaining hard cases are lateral joins and recursive CTEs, and we are honest that those sometimes need a human.

None of this is research. It is the craft of keeping a derived dataset honest while the source keeps moving. The unglamorous words matter: watermark, backfill, compaction, idempotency. If your lineage product cannot explain those four, it is a demo. The rest of the vocabulary — ontology, embedding, copilot — can wait until the forklifts work.

When we onboard a new engineer we do not start with the graph UI. We start with a failed backfill. We ask them to find which snapshot introduced a breaking schema change, which downstream dashboard went stale, and whether the importer retried or silently dropped the event. That drill teaches the real architecture faster than any diagram. The diagram is a map. The backfill is the terrain.

Caching is another place where taste shows. We cache schema hashes in Redis with a short TTL and a longer stale-while-revalidate window. The point is not to be clever. The point is to survive a thundering herd when a popular table lands a new snapshot at 2 a.m. If the cache is empty, one worker computes, the others wait on a lock, and everyone else reads the previous answer. Eventual consistency here is a feature. Analysts would rather see yesterday's lineage than a spinning wheel.

I keep a note on my desk: never let the graph become the product. The product is the question an on-call engineer asks at 3 a.m. — what broke, and what else will break if I rerun this job? If the graph cannot answer that in under a minute, we have built a museum.
